title: Binary
objective: After this level you can explain how ones and zeros can stand for numbers, letters and pictures.
summary: A switch is on or off, so computers count in binary: each place is worth double and 8 bits make a byte. Letters and pixel colors are stored as numbers.

cards.headline: The words you are reading are stored as 0s and 1s.
cards.body: So are your photos and your music. A computer stores numbers, letters, colors, pictures and sounds with just two symbols. How can two symbols spell out all of that?

cards.headline: Why only two?
cards.body: A computer is full of tiny electronic switches, and a switch has two states. Remember Level 4: a switch either closes the loop or leaves a gap. On stands for 1, off for 0. That two-symbol code is called binary ("bi" means two), and each single 0 or 1 is a bit. Everything else is built from bits.

mascot.line: A light switch has been speaking binary your whole life. It just never said much.

cards.headline: Counting with doubles
cards.body: In everyday numbers each place is worth ten times the one to its right. In binary each place is worth double: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128. To write a number, switch on the places that add up to it. 5 is 4 + 1, so it's 101. Eight bits make a byte, running from 00000000 to 11111111: 256 patterns, for the numbers 0 to 255.

cards.headline: Letters and pictures are numbers in disguise
cards.body: Give every character a number and text becomes binary. In the ASCII code, one byte stands for one letter, digit or punctuation mark: lowercase a is 01100001. Pictures work the same way. A photo is a grid of tiny dots called pixels, and each dot's color is stored as numbers. Your favorite photo is, underneath, a very long list of numbers.

cards.headline: Binary: decoded
learned: A switch is on (1) or off (0), so computers use binary
Each binary place is worth double: 1, 2, 4, 8 and so on
Eight bits make a byte: 256 patterns
Letters and pixel colors are stored as numbers

questions.prompt: In the ASCII code, how much space does a single letter such as lowercase a take up?

options.label: One bit
options.rationale: One bit is a single 0 or 1: only two patterns.

options.label: One pixel
options.rationale: Pixels are dots in a picture.

options.label: 256 bytes
options.rationale: 256 is how many patterns one byte can make.

questions.explanation: ASCII is an 8-bit code: one byte per letter. Lowercase a is 01100001.

questions.prompt: With binary place values of 8, 4, 2 and 1, which four-bit pattern stands for the number 6?
questions.explanation: 6 is 4 + 2, so switch on the 4s place and the 2s place: 0110.

questions.prompt: Level 4's switch either closes the loop or leaves a gap. Why does that make binary a natural fit for computers?

options.label: Each switch has exactly two states: on is 1, off is 0
Switches can count to ten on their own
options.rationale: A switch has only two states.

options.label: Binary needs no electricity at all
Open switches store extra energy for later
options.rationale: An open switch just stops the current.

questions.explanation: A computer's tiny switches are on or off, so a two-symbol code, 1 and 0, matches them exactly.
